comments.text:
I'm still on a 2080ti but I don't even care much to upgrade it at this point because getting an OLED feels like way more of an upgrade than if I spent thousands on the latest GPU. It makes all the older games I play look so much better than any graphical upgrade could ever achieve. I finally went back to Bioshock and it's stupid how good it looks with the Luma mod enabling native HDR. Even just auto HDR is good on the games it supports. I'll take Halo at 250fps HDR any day over the performance riddled mess a modern AAA title provides. But even in those games I don't care as much as I used to about running ultra settings. I just want it to look presentable enough to let the monitor do the work making it pop. There are so many great new games from AA and indie devs that run perfectly and for those an OLED is a huge upgrade compared to a new GPU. Boltgun 2 for example.

Worst case whenever there's a AAA game I'm interested in with the usual PC issues I just hook up the Series X to my monitor and play on that since at least most games will play stable enough on performance mode and the monitor helps make up for any visual downgrade. But generally I've been playing games with stylized graphics over "realism" and they look incredible with a good OLED when compared to forced RT at 30fps with constant boiling artifacts.

Online you'll sometimes see people talk down about HDR and stuff but I guarantee they've never seen it for themselves. But I don't blame people too much for not understanding what it's actually like when it's constantly poorly marketed and their opinions are colored by a LED TV with like 400 nits claiming to have HDR. I thought my mini LED TV with local dimming looked good but HDR didn't seem like that big of a deal. Then I got an OLED and realized that TV could barely even be considered HDR. There's still people who think HDR is just another word for bloom or some color thing.

I'm excited to get back into some classic horror games now that the blacks aren't washed out and flashlights are actually like real blinding flashlights. I intend to play Amnesia: The Bunker and it's gonna be fuckin terrifying how dark the bunker is.

comments.text:
Here’s my advice:

The latest QD-OLED panels are 5th-gen and feature a full RGB-stripe subpixel layout. However, they’re not available in 4K yet, so you’re stuck with lower pixel density (PPI). Personally, I’d wait a few months for a 32-inch 4K 5th-gen QD-OLED rather than buy one of the recently released 4th-gen WOLED monitors, which also feature the new RGB-stripe layout.

QD-OLED is generally considered the better choice for gaming visuals, especially when it comes to HDR colors and overall image quality.

When buying a gaming monitor, I’d focus on three things: panel technology, panel generation, and what your PC can comfortably run.

For demanding games at 4K or 5K, I’d personally recommend an RTX 5090. An RTX 5080 is still powerful, but you’ll have to lower or disable certain graphics settings in some games to maintain high frame rates. Obviously, that matters less in lightweight games like Valorant, which are much easier to run.

Beyond the panel itself, pay attention to the monitor’s physical controls, OSD (on-screen display), and overall usability. Personally, I’d avoid Samsung monitors.

One thing worth understanding is that brands like MSI and ASUS often use the same underlying OLED panels from the same manufacturers. So if both brands offer a monitor using the same generation and model of QD-OLED panel, the differences generally come down to things like the power supply, cooling, firmware, OSD, physical controls, build quality, and warranty.

In other words, don’t choose a monitor based on the brand name alone. Choose the panel first, then compare how each manufacturer implements it.

It’s not even just about image quality or contrast - it’s about how it actually feels in action. OLED delivers lightning-fast response times with zero motion blur, no ghosting, and no smearing. When you're using a mouse, that instant responsiveness makes the cursor and camera movement feel uniquely direct in a way you just can't even get on a OLED TV with a controller. For PC players it's easily the most impactful hardware upgrade of recent years.

comments.text:
OLED is so great for gaming, burn in is not much of an issue anymore. Only the most extreme usage with high brightness on static content will cause it nowadays.
When I got my first QD OLED which had a 3rd gen samsung panel I played Arc Raiders for hundreds of hours at max brightness without doing much else inbetween and even then there was not any visible image retention on hud elements.

Now I have a LG C6 Tandem OLED tv as a monitor and it features even better protections against burn in, much higher brightness and better color volume. The estimated half life of the pixels on single layer oled models is 50 000 - 100 000 hours according to the pace the pixels degrade on Rtings tests.
This means if you treat your display well and we assume the panel lasts for 50 000 hours it will last 17 years if you use it 8 hours every single day. Tandem OLED degrades at roughly half the rate so that is over 30 years before the pixels is at 50% brightness compared to new. It does not mean 30 years without image retention or burn in but it will take a very long time and that tv/monitor would likely be replaced way before you get issues.

With this display I get the same brightness and even more than some mini led monitors I have owned while retaining the perfect black levels and the superior motion clarity. Other display technologies are too slow when it comes to pixel response time. They don't change colors nearly as fast as the panels refresh rate.

Just one thing. It is very important when using SDR (rec 709 color space) to clamp these panels into that color space acordingly in order to prevent oversaturation of colors. Since sRGB modes on these OLED monitors are usually broken (essential options are locked out or gamma is not set correctly) you have novideo.srgb for NVIDIA cards and color clamp for AMD in their control panel.

As far as BURN-IN goes, OLED panels use organic, flurescent light emitters so degradation is inevitable, however, people think that burn-in is directly related to degradation, when in reality it is simply a result of UNEVEN panel wear which makes it apparent in real life usage. So think of it like this. Degradataion is inevitable and expected, and all these panel protections do is work around it to make it as even across the screen as possible. So as long as you dont play competitive games for thousands of hours and/or use static elements on your screen (like desktop icons, taskbar, browser title bar etc) you should not expect to have uneven/localized pixel wear (burn-in). But yo udo have to take precautions like hiding taskbar, if not hiding, then at least shifting desktop icons form time to time and when browsing either using ful lscreen mode or using windowed mode and moving it yourself from time to time. DArk/black theme is not really as important as even pixel wear. Bu using a black theme everywhere you will maybe save couple of wats of electricity, but if you have bright static elements you will cause uneven ware one way or another.

I have a 3rd gen QD-OLED panel, 32" 240 Hz.  I have over 3400 hours on it so far, have all the anti-burn-in stuff turned on (unnoticeable, btw), and while I try to keep up with pixel refreshes every 4 hours I have only done about 70% of those because of long gaming sessions.  I check my monitor periodically with varying shades of gray backgrounds and have yet to find ANY evidence of burn-in.  QD-OLED has the best color saturation, the extra backlight in WOLED tends to wash out colors in HDR mode.  The response time of OLED monitors is both a blessing and a curse.  If you're going to run frame rates of 140 and up, you're golden.  Once you drop down below 80-90 fps the motion clarity really shows the low frame rates.

OLED really shows off one of the most dramatic visual improvements: proper luminance from black to full white.  I'm a home theater enthusiast and calibrate my own stuff, I have a colorimeter and a spectrophotometer.  These days most televisions and monitors are very good with color calibration right out of the box.  Where calibration has the most impact is getting light output, or luminance, set correctly across the intensity range from 0% to 100%.  This gives you the best contrast levels and the best upgrade to the performance.  A note on HDR:  most peak 1000 modes on QD-OLED's will end up dimming overall light levels at lower percentages in order to make 1000 nits.  If you see a scene darkening overall when you switch from True HDR mode to Peak 1000, you're seeing the effect in action.  I like more accurate lighting levels so I run my monitor at True HDR 400.  If you're looking for the best HDR in a game that doesn't have real HDR, RenoDX is a great option.

This is all very interesting, of course, but in the final analysis, if you cut through all the fluff, an OLED only outperforms a good IPS or QLED in a completely dark room, in scenes with a full black level. Otherwise, if you have a good IPS or QLED panel, you won't notice any difference. However, pixel shifting is clearly visible if you're focused on one point (shooter or working with documents), and you constantly need to try to remove all static images as much as possible. The start menu, the browser's top bar, and so on and so forth. And it's a constant hassle. They still burn out, maybe more slowly than before, but still. And what about turning it off every 4-6 hours to clear the pixels? That's just brutal: you're in the middle of a heated battle, and the monitor just keeps turning off. Sure, you can delay it, but then the pixels will burn out. Overall, I'm not discouraging you from buying one. You might use it for the first couple of days in some scenarios where OLED looks great, but then you'll get tired of it. Even in daylight, even in a 1:1 comparison, there's no difference.

By the way, it's worth noting that OLEDs often have issues with grayscale, with gradients and uneven fills. Personally, this really irritates me. I haven't encountered this with other types of panels.

Anyway, thanks for the video.

Recently upgraded to an OLED myself. The one I got is a LG 27GX704A-B. A 27 inch Tandom OLED with glossy finish. So lights reflect off it more. But since My PC/Monitor setup is under a loft bed there's not much light to reflect off. OLEDs with no anti-glare on them tend to be brighter and better blacks/contrast so that's what I got. My unit runs at 1440p at 240hz so not a full 4k display but my GTX 1060 would struggle to run games at that resolution anyways so 1440p is better for my more budget oriented machine. Heck even Fall Guys can't reach the full 240FPS the monitor can handle so I still plan to upgrade that eventually to something that should handle that. A full 4k capable video card is still way out of my price range though. :P

Before this I was mainly using a CRT monitor because yeah...LCDs just don't cut it for me. CRTs still have OLEDs beat in terms of response times and motion clarity. They also handle lower resolutions better since they are analog and don't have a native resolution. So when I did decide to upgrade it would be OLED or nothing. CRTs main disadvantage is brightness and resolution. Only really high end hard to find CRT monitors can come close to the resolutions modern OLEDs get. They also can't get to as high refresh rates...but then again CRTs were so good with motion clarity that you could easily get away with anything past like 67hz. (You start to notice flicker if you are at 60hz or less with CRTs but thankfully most of them you can run a bit faster then that to avoid it). Definite trade offs. I'd say these days CRT monitors would be great for retro setups but for the main PC in your room, OLED is the only acceptable monitors to be using in the modern age. :P

comments.text: Hi, Principal Research Scientist here, I have a PhD in Materials Science and Engineering and create these technologies. I’m happy you’re loving OLED and I’d really encourage you to look into RGB Mini LED. Burn in is not so much an issue as peak HDR brightness is. Most games are graded to 1000 nits or above brightness and QD-OLED can’t sustain this level on a full screen window. OLED also loses peak brightness very quickly and permanently. Your monitor won’t be nearly as bright year 2 as it is year 1. This is an issue because the starting brightness is already low. It looks nice to you due to the contrast but RGB Mini LED achieves this as well but at higher peak brightness levels. Enjoy your screen for the time being but I’d recommend RGB Mini LED instead! Once other tech like Q-DEL and MicroLED take off, OLED will be dead as there will be no advantages to owning a low lifespan piece of tech

Effectively infinite contrast is great sure, but this isn't anything new. We already had plasma displays that could do the same decades ago.
I've been using OLED displays for over 14x years already and can't wait to move on to something better.

OLEDs are far from display nirvana. They suffer from panel uniformity issues and artifacts, noise/dithering and poor gradation near black.

They're also a sample & hold based technology, so the motion clarity is always going to be bad without BFI at a very high panel framerate, since OLEDs are self-emissive you can't just strobe the backlight like with an LCD whose light source can be addressed independently.

Yes I know someone is going to say "oh but OLED has instant pixel response, how can you say that!1!", this is not relevant - learn how the human visual system works, even at 240 Hz just pan around in an FPS game and it's a blurry mess.

comments.text:
The thing with most of these OLED fanboys is... that they do not have any experience whatsoever with MiniLED other than watching it in a store with basically the worst viewing conditions.
That said, if you're using a TV as a monitor, a good MiniLED is great. No risk of burn-in and it gets brighter as well. Black levels are very close to OLED, but there may be some blooming (and how much depends on the MiniLED. Something like the Bravia 9 has pretty much none for most part, but something like one of those cheaper bright HiSense or TCL TV's go for extra brightness at the cost of having some blooming).

If you intend to buy a monitor... well, MiniLED monitors are still quite a bit behind their TV counterparts in terms of display quality. But you do get a higher refresh rate. Well, OLED monitors are behind as well compared to their TV's, but not as much. And if you're sitting up close to a monitor, the flaws of MiniLED and strength of OLED will be quite noticeable.

But OLED still hasn't solved burn-in. If you like to pump up your brightness and use your monitor or TV a lot, it's probably best to avoid OLED because it'll get burn-in in about 2-3 years. If you're more of a casual user and are willing to turn down the settings, OLED is a good choice. As for me, I expect my expensive displays to be a work horse, not a prancing horse. Spending big bucks on an expensive display only to use it with half of its potential 90% of the time? To me that's a waste of money.

comments.text: It's not an extra layer of quantum dots, it's that the color filter is made out of quantum dots for red and green and because the light source is blue for that subpixel color you have just a hole. This is an improvement over LG's WOLED that uses white light with a white subpixel that boosts brightness, but what you get is when you measure the display using a spectrograph (to get a waveform of the colors of the light) is that this white light washes the light output together whereas with QD-OLED you get very pure peaks of R, G and B. Though phone/tablet/handheld/laptop screens are even better because they don't use a color filter at all and having individual emitters per subpixel which gets you even tighter peaks per color. LCD TVs often apply a quantum dot enhancement film to improve color performance, but that is not the case here. A quick 2 minute Google search could have told you that information
